lms_catalog.title: Introduction to the Open Compute Project
lms_catalog.short_description: Discover the OCP Community, explore open infrastructure, and plan your next step in adoption or participation.
lms_catalog.overview: Discover how the Open Compute Project (OCP) brings people and organizations together to develop and share open infrastructure. This introductory course explores OCP's origins, Community, governance and contribution process, then connects Open Rack and cooling concepts to practical adoption decisions. Expert videos, narrated explanations, animations and knowledge checks help you find relevant resources and choose a useful next step. No engineering prerequisites are required.
lms_catalog.duration_note: Includes narration, expert videos, reading, activities and knowledge checks. Optional linked courses and external study are additional.

modules.summary: Explore the practical problems that inspired OCP, its five tenets, and the value of open collaboration. Consider how shared designs can support different roles and why evidence matters when evaluating their benefits.

Understand the roles of the OCP Foundation, governance bodies, project leaders and contributors. Follow the contribution path from a shared problem to review and publication, and identify appropriate ways to participate in the OCP Community.

Connect rack design, power distribution, heat removal and facility requirements. Explore Open Rack and cooling approaches, recognize important interfaces and constraints, and find specialist Academy courses for deeper study.

Use OCP recognition programs, the Marketplace and contribution resources within their stated scope. Define a bounded pilot with clear responsibilities and decision criteria, then choose technical or OCP Community Orientation courses that match your next step.

modules.title: The OCP Origins
modules.subtitle: Why shared designs and open collaboration matter.

slides.title: Open ideas. Shared progress.
slides.subtitle: Understand OCP, explore its community, and find your next step.
slides.transcript: The Open Compute Project, or OCP, is a community that shares designs and knowledge to improve computing infrastructure. It brings people who use technology together with people who build it, so they can solve common problems. In this course, you’ll discover how that collaboration works, recognize a few important technologies, and choose a practical first step for your own work.

slides.title: Your route into OCP
slides.subtitle: About 45 minutes · no engineering prerequisites
slides.media_embed:
Matty Bakkeren
Founder, Momenthesis
Course author and contributor
slides.transcript: We thank Matty Bakkeren, founder of Momenthesis, for developing the original course material and sharing his expertise. Start with the origins and purpose. Then meet the community and learn how contributions develop. Explore Open Rack and cooling as examples of shared engineering, before planning a small, evidence-based adoption step. Allow about forty-five minutes for the core course, including all six recordings and the activities. The linked specialist courses are optional further study.

slides.title: A practical problem became a shared opportunity

bullets.text: 2011: OCP launched around shared infrastructure designs.
The original challenge: efficient growth of internet services.
The continuing approach: publish, review, reuse and improve.

slides.transcript: OCP began in 2011, following work to improve the efficiency of Facebook’s growing computing infrastructure. Facebook, now Meta, opened designs and helped launch the project with other founding participants. The original challenge was scaling internet services efficiently. Today’s AI workloads create additional demands, but they did not cause the project’s founding. The lasting idea is to share useful design work so more organizations can examine it, adapt it under its license, and improve it together.

slides.title: The OCP origin story

figure.caption: Matty Bakkeren’s introduction to the origins and open-design approach.

entries.text: They weren’t just running out of space. They were burning power on things that didn’t matter.
The problems of traditional data centers. Thick plastic bezels. Restricted air vents.
What if we designed a data center like a single, giant computer?
The result was the vanity-free server
No bezels. Centralized power. Optimized airflow.
Its open innovation engine, it supports and contributes
With the rise of AI and heat-dense workloads

slides.video_transcript: To understand why OCP matters today, you have to go back to the critical point that started it all. In 2010, the rise of mobile computing, social media, and cloud storage caused internet traffic to explode. But the hardware powering it was stuck in the past. In 2011, Meta, formerly Facebook, hit a wall. They were growing so fast that traditional data center technology literally could not keep up. They weren't just running out of space, they were burning power on things that didn't matter. At the time, every server was a black box. Proprietary designs, gratuitous plastic bezels, logos that blocked airflow, and power supplies that were horribly inefficient. If they wanted to scale, rules had to be broken. So, a small team of engineers at Facebook asked a radical question. What if we designed a data center like a single giant computer? What if we stripped away the vanity and focused only on efficiency? That question launched the Open Compute Project or OCP. OCP took the schematics for the most efficient server in the world, and we didn't patent them, we published them. We invited the world to hack our hardware. The result was the vanity-free server. We removed the plastic, we centralized the power, we optimized the airflow. It wasn't just cheaper to build, it was 38% more efficient and 24% less expensive to run. This model works so well for a reason. The hyperscalers run into the physical limits of IT infrastructure years before anyone else because of their size, scale operations, and relentless performing demands. Also, by solving these extreme scaling challenges with the industry and an open mindset first and then publishing those blueprints, we hand those engineer solutions directly to the rest of the market, accelerating adoption and driving new industry benchmarks. OCP is not a standards body itself, but by the nature of its open innovation engine, it supports and contributes to standardization. Today, OCP isn't just for hyperscalers, it's a $132 billion ecosystem. From the co-location facility down the street to the edge of the telecom network, open hardware is the standard for high performance computing. But this isn't just history. With the rise of AI and heat dense workloads, the principles we established in 2011. Efficiency, openness, impact, scale, and sustainability are the only way we will survive the next decade. So welcome to the community. Let's take a look at the specs.

slides.title: One shared problem, many useful implementations

figure.alt: Shared design work supports different implementations; operating experience improves the next revision.
figure.caption: Shared design work supports different implementations; operating experience improves the next revision.

slides.transcript: Imagine three organizations solving the same equipment-service problem separately. Each spends time defining the interface and discovering similar limitations. Open collaboration starts by making the common requirement visible. A team proposes a shared design, and others review the assumptions, identify problems, and suggest improvements. Once published under the applicable license, that work can support different implementations. Experience from those implementations feeds back into the next revision. The gain is shared learning and a reusable starting point. It does not remove the need to test a particular product in a particular environment.

slides.title: Five tenets guide the work

cards.title: Efficiency
cards.body: Use energy, materials, space and effort well.

cards.title: Impact
cards.body: Address a meaningful shared need.

cards.title: Openness
cards.body: Make useful design knowledge available under clear terms.

cards.title: Scale
cards.body: Support repeatable use beyond a one-off prototype.

cards.title: Sustainability
cards.body: Consider environmental effects across the life cycle.

slides.transcript: OCP describes its work through five tenets: efficiency, impact, openness, scale, and sustainability. Think of them as questions to ask about a proposal. Does it use resources well? Does it address a meaningful shared need? Can others understand and use the contribution under its terms? Can the approach be deployed at a useful scale? And how does it affect environmental outcomes over its life? These ideas guide the community, while the current contribution process defines the specific submission requirements.

slides.title: Where open work can help you

cards.title: Architect
cards.body: Compare interfaces and implementation choices.

cards.title: Developer
cards.body: Reuse documented work; focus on your distinctive problem.

cards.title: Operations team
cards.body: Bring maintenance and service evidence into design reviews.

slides.transcript: An architect can compare documented interfaces before selecting a platform. A developer can reuse a contributed design instead of starting every detail from scratch. An operations team can share service experience that makes the next design easier to maintain. Open hardware makes useful design information available under stated terms. Interoperability is a separate question: whether the selected parts work together as required. Shared interfaces help, but a common label alone does not establish compatibility, supplier support, or a safe installation.

slides.title: New workloads, the same collaborative habit

bullets.text: Workload choices affect equipment and facilities together.
Power, cooling, networks and service access interact.
Shared learning can connect different organizations’ expertise.

slides.transcript: AI is one reason computing infrastructure is changing quickly. More demanding equipment can put pressure on power delivery, heat removal, networking, and service access at the same time. Those connections make collaboration valuable: a component improvement is only useful when the surrounding system can support it. In the next recording, the speakers discuss building AI hardware. Listen for the relationship between equipment design and the people who integrate and operate it.

slides.title: Look for evidence behind the promise

bullets.text: Ask: compared with what, where, and under which workload?
Separate design potential from measured deployment results.
Include repair, reuse and support in life-cycle decisions.

slides.transcript: Open designs can support better choices, but outcomes depend on the implementation. A claim about energy use, cost, deployment speed, or reuse should identify what was measured and under what conditions. Circularity means keeping products, components, and materials useful for longer through approaches such as repair and reuse. A modular design may help, but a real circularity plan also needs spare parts, support, and a viable next use. Treat broad benefit claims as starting questions, not universal guarantees.

modules.title: The OCP Ecosystem & Governance
modules.subtitle: Find the right people and understand the contribution path.

slides.title: The community behind the designs
slides.subtitle: Roles, projects and a practical path to participation.
slides.transcript: OCP brings together operators, suppliers, researchers, and people with different technical interests. This module shows where that work happens and how an idea can become a published contribution.

slides.title: Find your place in the community
objectives: Distinguish Foundation, Steering Committee and project roles.
Find a project connected to your problem.
Separate contribution publication from product recognition.
slides.transcript: You’ll distinguish the main organizational roles, choose a relevant project, and follow a contribution from its initial proposal to publication.

slides.title: Different roles, connected responsibilities

cards.title: Foundation & Board
cards.body: Organizational support, programs and governance.

cards.title: Steering Committee
cards.body: Technical direction and contribution review.

cards.title: Project leads
cards.body: Coordinate work and guide proposals in their domains.

cards.title: Contributors
cards.body: Develop, review, test and improve shared work.

slides.transcript: The Foundation provides the organizational framework, programs, and support for the community. Its Board provides governance. The Steering Committee supports technical direction and contribution review. Project leads organize work within their domains, while contributors bring proposals, analysis, testing, documentation, and feedback. These roles connect rather than form a simple production line. A useful proposal often crosses project boundaries, so start with the relevant project leads and follow the current process.

slides.title: How the OCP Community works

figure.caption: Matty Bakkeren explains collaboration across the OCP Community.

entries.text: Putting thousands of engineers in a single room gets you lots of great ideas
But that brainpower needs to be properly channeled
The work of OCP happens in specialized project groups
Rack and Power. Cooling Environments. Open-source Networking.
The hyperscaler who runs the data center
The vendor who builds the hardware
Debate about the physics. Iterate on the designs. Solve problems together.
They are a panel of elected industry experts
List them on the Marketplace for the rest of the world to buy and deploy
The community identifies the bottleneck. The project groups design the solution. The committee ensures the quality.

slides.video_transcript: In 2011, we opened the black box and shared the blueprints, but blueprints don't build themselves. To actually change the industry, we needed an innovation engine that is powered by openness. What we needed was a community. Today, the Open Compute Project isn't just a library of specifications. It's a living community driven by a shared goal, creating open solutions for data center operators facing extreme scaling challenges. Putting thousands of engineers in a single room gets you lots of great ideas, but that brainpower needs to be properly channeled. So, the work of OCP happens in specialized project groups. You can think of these as engineering departments. You have teams dedicated entirely to Rack and Power, other focused on cooling environments, and others write open source networking specifications, and so there are many more. But this is where the magic happens. We put the hyperscaler who actually builds and runs these mega data centers in the same room as the vendor who builds the hardware and the industry that is using that same equipment. They argue about physics. They iterate on the designs, and they solve problems together before a single piece of metal is stamped. But it's not the wild west. Before any design becomes an official OCP standard, it has to get past the technical gatekeepers, the steering committee. They are a panel of elected industry experts who ruthlessly review any submission. If a design doesn't meet the strict tenets for efficiency, impact, openness, scalability, and sustainability, it goes right back to the drawing board. But once the committee approves the specification, it's locked in. Vendors can then manufacture the physical hardware. Earn the OCP Accepted mark. And list them on the marketplace for the rest of the world to see, buy, and deploy. The community identifies the bottleneck, the project groups design the solution, and the committee ensures the quality. That's how we move the industry forward. And now that you know how the engine works, let's talk about my favorite topic, hardware.

slides.title: A wider landscape than the rack

cards.title: Rack & Power
cards.body: Mechanical and electrical interfaces.

cards.title: Cooling Environments
cards.body: Heat-removal technologies and their interfaces.

cards.title: Server & Networking
cards.body: Computing platforms and connectivity.

cards.title: Data Center Facility
cards.body: The site infrastructure around the equipment.

cards.title: Cross-cutting work
cards.body: Management, firmware, security and sustainability.

slides.transcript: OCP work spans connected layers. Rack and Power addresses shared rack and power interfaces. Cooling Environments addresses thermal technologies. Server and Networking projects focus on computing and connectivity. Data Center Facility work considers the infrastructure around the equipment. Hardware Management, security, firmware, and sustainability work add capabilities that cross these layers. The online community directory is the current map. Use the problem you want to solve to find the right group, rather than assuming every topic belongs to the rack project.

slides.title: From a useful idea to a published contribution

figure.alt: The exact route depends on the contribution type; product recognition is a separate process.
figure.caption: The exact route depends on the contribution type; product recognition is a separate process.

entries.text: Published work can receive later revisions.

slides.transcript: Suppose your team has learned how to improve a cooling interface. First, discuss the problem with the relevant project and submit the required proposal information. Agree the contribution type, scope, and licensing route. Next, develop the draft using the applicable guidance and invite community review. Review can send you back to revise the proposal; that is useful work, not a failed process. Follow the required project and Steering Committee approvals, including any applicable notice period. Publication makes the accepted contribution available, and later experience can lead to a new revision. A vendor’s product-recognition application is a separate path, not an automatic result of publishing a design.

slides.title: A contribution and a product are different things

cards.title: Published contribution
cards.body: Shared design knowledge with a defined scope and terms.

cards.title: Product recognition
cards.body: A program relationship between a product and relevant contributions.

cards.title: Deployment decision
cards.body: Your evidence that the selected system meets its requirements.

slides.transcript: A contribution is shared work published through OCP’s process. It might be a specification, design, guideline, or another supported document type. A product is a particular implementation supplied and supported by an organization. Product recognition relates that product to the relevant OCP contribution and program requirements. Neither publication nor recognition establishes that your complete installation is ready. Keep the documents, the product revision, and the deployment evidence connected, but do not treat them as the same approval.

slides.title: Start with a useful, manageable contribution

bullets.text: Read a project’s current scope and meeting information.
Bring a specific requirement, question or piece of evidence.
Check current membership terms before making commitments.

slides.transcript: You can begin by reading a project’s public materials, joining its open discussions, and asking a focused question. Participation in community activities and formal organizational membership are different. Membership provides defined benefits and responsibilities, which can change over time. The linked membership guide describes participation benefits. Confirm current terms with OCP before making an organizational decision. You can also contribute by reviewing a draft, reporting test results, improving documentation, or sharing an operational problem that others recognize.

slides.title: Try it: where would you take this problem?

bullets.text: Problem: a cooling connection is difficult to service.
Start with Cooling Environments; involve related interface owners.
Bring the conditions, observations and desired improvement.

slides.transcript: Your team finds that a cooling connector is awkward to service in a populated rack. Start with the cooling community, and involve Rack and Power where the mechanical arrangement matters. Bring the interface description, service conditions, and what you observed. A vague request to improve cooling is hard to act on; a bounded problem with evidence gives the community something to review. If the work also affects monitoring, involve the relevant management expertise.

modules.title: OCP Technologies — Open Rack & Cooling
modules.subtitle: Connect equipment, power, heat removal and the facility.

slides.title: Meet the technology as a system
slides.subtitle: Open Rack and cooling are examples within a broader ecosystem.
slides.transcript: Open Rack and cooling make open collaboration tangible. We’ll use them to connect the equipment that does the work with the power, heat removal, and operations that support it.

slides.title: Connect the important relationships
objectives: Describe the roles of a rack, power distribution and cooling.
Compare cooling approaches without assuming one fits every site.
slides.transcript: Focus on what each part does and what must work together. Detailed design and installation belong in the specialist courses and the applicable engineering process.

slides.title: Power arrives. Heat leaves. Interfaces connect.

figure.alt: Conceptual relationships, not an installation schematic. Both power delivery and heat removal need complete paths.
figure.caption: Conceptual relationships, not an installation schematic. Both power delivery and heat removal need complete paths.

slides.transcript: Begin with computing equipment: servers, storage, and network devices perform useful work. The rack supports and organizes that equipment and its interfaces. Power travels from the facility through the selected conversion and distribution systems to the equipment. A busbar is a conductor used to distribute electrical power; in an Open Rack implementation it forms part of that path. Most electrical energy used by the equipment becomes heat that must leave through the intended cooling system. Some systems use air, some bring liquid close to selected components, and some use both. Management information helps operators observe the system, but measurement does not replace the physical capacity of power and cooling.

slides.title: Explore Open Rack

figure.caption: Matty Bakkeren introduces Open Rack architecture and its development.

entries.text: Legacy server. Limited motherboard space. Internal PSU. Restricted airflow path.
Creates two challenges: extreme weight, extreme heat
By introducing the Open Compute Project’s Universal Quick Disconnect standard
ORv3 allows server gear to be slid directly into the rack
We solved the power delivery bottleneck. But extracting that

slides.video_transcript: We've talked about the history and we've talked about the community. Now, let's get hands on. This is the Open Rack version 3 or ORv3. It's the physical foundation of the modern AI driven data centre. And to understand why it's built this way, you have to understand the architecture of power. In a traditional nineteen-inch rack, every server had its own power supply. It was plugged into a giant power strip known as a PDU. Early open racks solved this cable mess by replacing the power strips with a centralised twelve-volt busbar that was built right into the frame. This was fine for standard cloud servers pulling 10 to 15 kilowatts. But today's IA clusters demand 100 kilowatts or more per rack. If you try to push that much power at 12 volts, your current goes through the roof. It goes way beyond simple power loss. Pushing that much current through a 12 volt busbar would be catastrophic. It would melt the copper, sparks would fly and result in a complete system failure. So the rack and power project group changed the standard. ORv3 utilises a 48 volt DC busbar. By stepping up the voltage, we reduce the heat loss by 16 times. That means more power actually reaches the silicon instead of burning up in the infrastructure. We also totally reimagined power delivery. In a traditional setup, every single server has its own redundant power supply, which usually runs at a low, inefficient utilisation rate. ORv3 pulls that workload. It replaces dozens of individual power supplies with a single centralised power shelf loaded with modular rectifiers. By consolidating the AC to DC conversion for the entire rack, we drive the utilisation rate up and the power losses down. This centralised approach simplifies deployment. IT gear slides in and connects to the power spine without any manual wiring. No thick power cords blocking your exhaust air flow. Eliminating server PSUs frees up motherboard space, enabling denser compute and improved system airflow. But delivering that much power creates two secondary challenges, extreme weight and extreme heat. The physical frame of the ORv3 rack has been reinforced to handle the massive weight of modern GPU chassis. More importantly, the ORv3 frame futureproofs your data centre for the next generation of heat. It is designed to natively integrate liquid cooling manifolds right into the rack architecture. It introduces the Open Compute Universal Quick Disconnect Standard or UQD for short. ORv3 allows server gear to be slid directly into the rack, safely and seamlessly connecting its liquid cooling circuits without any drips. We solved the power delivery bottleneck, but extracting that heat is a whole different beast. Let's look at how we keep these racks from actually melting down.

slides.title: Shared interfaces, specific implementations

cards.title: Mechanical arrangement
cards.body: Fit, support, service access and handling.

cards.title: Electrical arrangement
cards.body: Conversion, distribution and equipment connections.

cards.title: Thermal arrangement
cards.body: Air and/or liquid paths with defined requirements.

slides.transcript: Open Rack describes shared approaches to arranging equipment and its supporting interfaces. Earlier versions established important mechanical and rack-level power ideas. Open Rack version three develops those interfaces for newer needs. High-power work addresses electrical capacity, while Open Rack Wide addresses the physical envelope. The names are not interchangeable ratings. A wider frame does not by itself provide more usable electrical power, and a power upgrade does not prove cooling readiness. Use the relevant specification and implementation documents to understand what a particular assembly supports.

slides.title: Why higher distribution voltage can help

bullets.text: Same power: 12 V → 48 V means one-quarter current.
Same resistance: I²R loss becomes one-sixteenth.
This is a simplified conductor-loss comparison—not whole-rack efficiency.

slides.transcript: For the same delivered electrical power, increasing voltage reduces current. In an ideal comparison, moving from 12 V to 48 V makes the current one quarter as large. Resistive loss follows current squared times resistance, so with the same conductor resistance, that particular loss becomes one sixteenth as large. This is not a claim that a complete rack becomes sixteen times more efficient. Real systems include conversion losses, connections, controls, operating limits, and many other design choices. The relationship explains a motivation, not a guaranteed system result.

slides.title: Explore cooling technologies

figure.caption: Matty Bakkeren compares ways to remove heat from computing equipment.

entries.text: For facilities that are not ready to pipe water directly into the servers, we use rear door heat exchangers
Rear door heat exchangers. Passive. Active. Fanwall. Liquid filled coil.
ORv3 is driven by three main hardware standardizations
21 inch width. Centralized power busbar. Liquid manifold stay-out zone.
Every ORv3 rack reserves a dedicated standardized physical space. Liquid manifolds.
This standardized manifold space perfectly enables direct liquid cooling
Direct liquid cooling. Cold liquid. Heat. Metal cold plates. Processor.
Zero-leak fluid connectors. Safely pumps a water and glycol mix directly to the silicon
This captures up to 80% of the heat
Our ultimate density solution requires immersion cooling
Entire servers are completely submerged. Non-conductive dielectric fluid.
The fluid touches every component. No blind-mate manifolds or hoses required.
Single-phase. Server. Dielectric fluid. Coolant-to-water heat exchange. Coolant pump. Cooling tower.
Two-phase. Warmer water output. Condenser. Condensation. Evaporated oil. Servers. Water pump. Water chiller unit. Cold water input.

slides.video_transcript: For decades, data centers relied on a simple principle to keep servers from melting down. Push cold air in the front and blow hot air out the back. But with the sheer density of modern AI silicon, air cooling has hit a wall. The heat cannot and transport fast enough. Air is simply a terrible conductor of heat. Liquid can capture and transport thousands of times more efficiently than air. To support AI clusters pushing 100 kilowatts or more compared to the standard 12 kilowatt rack. The OCP Cooling Environments project had to shift the industry standards. This transition happens in stages. For facilities that are not ready to pipe water directly into the servers, we use rear door heat exchangers, RDX. These come in two forms. Passive simply uses the liquid-filled coil. Active includes a fan wall to assist in the heat transfer, combining air and liquid cooling into one. The incredible success of the Open Rack v3 is driven by 3 main hardware standardizations. The 21 inch width, the centralized power busbar, and the liquid manifold stay-out zone. Every ORv3 rack reserves a dedicated standardized physical space strictly for liquid manifolds. In an industry with very few liquid standards, this provides a predictable plug and play architecture for fluid delivery. This standardized manifold space perfectly enables direct liquid cooling or DLC. Metal cold plates with microchannels are mounted right on top of the CPU and GPUs. Using high reliability zero leak fluid connectors, the rack mounted manifold safely pumps a water and glycol mix directly to the silicon. This captures up to 80% of the heat exactly where it's generated. While liquid cooling maximizes the potential of the standard ORv3 rack. Our ultimate solution requires a completely different physical architecture, immersion cooling. Instead of sliding it into a vertical rack, entire servers are now completely submerged into a horizontal tank of nonconductive dielectric fluid. Because the fluid physically touches every component, CPU GPU, memory and network, there are no blind mate manifolds or hoses required. In a single phase, the fluid absorbs the heat. In a two-phase, the extreme heat actually boils the fluid, and the resulting phase change allows the vapor to condense and cool the hardware at an unmatched scale. Whether it's cold plate or a full immersion tank, liquid cooling is no longer a science experiment, it's a survival requirement. Now the hardware is built, the specs are published, the only thing left to do is to deploy it.

slides.title: Four approaches, different integration questions

cards.title: Air cooling
cards.body: Air carries heat to the room or facility cooling system.

cards.title: Rear-door heat exchanger
cards.body: Transfers exhaust-air heat into a liquid loop.

cards.title: Direct-to-chip
cards.body: Cold plates cool selected components; residual air cooling may remain.

cards.title: Immersion
cards.body: Compatible equipment operates in a suitable dielectric fluid.

slides.transcript: Air cooling carries heat away in airflow to the room or facility cooling system. A rear-door heat exchanger transfers heat from the exhaust air into a liquid loop. Direct-to-chip cooling brings coolant through cold plates attached to selected components; other components may still need air. A coolant distribution unit, or CDU, manages a cooling-loop interface, depending on the design. Immersion places compatible equipment in a dielectric fluid designed not to conduct electricity under its specified conditions. These approaches are alternatives and combinations, not a mandatory ladder of progress. Each needs suitable equipment, materials, service procedures, and a complete path for rejecting heat.

slides.title: Choose from requirements—not a universal threshold

bullets.text: Match equipment requirements to site conditions.
Include maintenance, reliability and environmental tradeoffs.
Check the complete heat path, including any air-cooled remainder.

slides.transcript: There is no single rack-power number that determines the right cooling technology for every deployment. Start with the equipment’s requirements and the site’s available conditions. Then consider reliability, maintenance skills, water and energy use, material compatibility, and the full life cycle. A cooling method that works well in one configuration can be unsuitable in another. Compare evidence for the same workload and operating conditions, and identify who is responsible for each interface.

slides.title: The surrounding ecosystem matters

cards.title: Facility
cards.body: Space, access, electrical supply and heat rejection.

cards.title: Digital operations
cards.body: Management, networking, firmware and security.

cards.title: Life cycle
cards.body: Manufacture, operation, maintenance, reuse and recovery.

slides.transcript: A working system also needs compatible networking, management, security, and firmware. The facility must support delivery, placement, electrical capacity, and heat rejection. Sustainability decisions include operating resources and the impacts of making, maintaining, and eventually reusing or recovering equipment. These concerns cross organizational boundaries. OCP’s wider community helps teams share knowledge across them, while other standards organizations contribute complementary work. Follow the relevant project and alliance resources when your question extends beyond the rack.

slides.title: Try it: what else must you ask?

bullets.text: What power and cooling conditions must the site provide?
What remains air cooled?
How will installation, service and monitoring work?

slides.transcript: A team proposes new liquid-cooled servers because the rack footprint fits. Before treating that as a deployment plan, ask what electrical supply the equipment needs, what cooling conditions must be delivered, and how the remaining heat is removed. Ask how technicians will install and service it, and how alarms and operating limits are monitored. The useful habit is to connect the interfaces. A fit check is one input, not the whole decision.

slides.video_transcript: So we have covered the history, the rack architecture, and the cooling specifications. Now it's time to map out your actual deployment journey. And that journey starts with a rigorous facility assessment. Before you buy a single piece of hardware, you must evaluate your site against some critical readiness factors. In general, there are 3 areas that are the focus of this assessment. First, power density. Can your facility support the required power density? Second, thermal capacity. Are you prepared to route liquid cooling manifolds? And third, physical weight. Fully populated ORv3 racks are incredibly heavy. So your structural floors must be able to support this massive load in a safe way. Now, once your facility is cleared, your next stop is the OCP marketplace. This is your central hub for procuring verified hardware. You'll want to look exclusively for the OCP Accepted badge. These are officially recognized products that strictly adhere to the designs published in our database. And remember, OCP Accepted gear guarantees proven efficiency, whether you're building a new data center or replacing legacy 19-inch racks. But what if your current facility fails the assessment? If your floors can't handle the weight, or you lack the cooling infrastructure. You don't have to abandon the transition. You can migrate your operations to an OCP Ready co-location facilities. These are heavily audited third party sites that are purpose built specifically to house OCP hardware. Transitioning to open infrastructure is a massive undertaking, but you don't have to do it alone. You are now part of the community and you have access to a rich ecosystem. The marketplace is filled with certified OCP solution providers. These are professional services companies and system integrators that are specifically trained to assess your readiness, design your architecture, and physically deploy the hardware on your behalf. The community has already done the heavy engineering for you. Your next step is to see it through for yourself. Browse the digital OCP marketplace to find your hardware and solution providers or book a visit to a physical OCP experience center to see this technology running in person. Welcome to the Open Compute ecosystem.
slides.caption: Current program clarification: OCP Ready™ uses facility self-certification; OCP does not conduct an on-site audit. Recognition is not a guarantee of your deployment’s compatibility.

slides.title: Read recognition at the right level

cards.title: OCP Accepted
cards.body: Product recognition against the relevant contribution and program scope.

cards.title: OCP Ready™
cards.body: Facility self-certification; not an OCP on-site audit.

cards.title: Deployment acceptance
cards.body: Evidence for your selected configuration, site and workload.

slides.transcript: OCP Accepted identifies product recognition tied to relevant approved OCP contributions and program requirements. It does not guarantee a particular deployment’s efficiency or that every recognized product works with every other one. OCP Ready is a facility program using self-certification against its requirements; OCP’s current guidance says it does not conduct an on-site audit. Read the scope and supporting information, then ask what your workload and configuration still need to establish. Product recognition, facility information, and your deployment acceptance serve different purposes.

slides.title: Use the Marketplace to discover and investigate

bullets.text: Find a candidate product, service, solution or facility.
Read its scope and request configuration-specific evidence.
Confirm support, integration responsibilities and acceptance criteria.

slides.transcript: The Marketplace helps you discover products, solutions, services, and facilities connected with the OCP ecosystem. It is a starting point for a conversation with a provider. Check the exact product and revision, the contribution it relates to, what is included, and the support available. Request evidence for your own operating conditions. A listing is not a substitute for supplier due diligence, an integration plan, or the checks required by your organization.

slides.title: Make the next decision smaller and better informed

figure.alt: A pilot is a learning decision with clear criteria—not an automatic commitment to scale.
figure.caption: A pilot is a learning decision with clear criteria—not an automatic commitment to scale.

slides.transcript: Begin with the workload and the problem you want to improve. Record the site constraints and what success would look like. Next, discover candidate designs, products, and partners, then qualify the interfaces and responsibilities. Plan a bounded pilot with measurements and a way to stop or recover if requirements are not met. During the pilot, compare results with the agreed criteria. Use that evidence to expand, revise, or stop. Share useful findings with the community where appropriate. Starting small is valuable because it makes learning manageable, not because a small installation needs no engineering review.

slides.title: Try it: give the pilot a clear job

bullets.text: Purpose: test one defined improvement under representative conditions.
Evidence: performance, service effort, power, thermal behavior and support.
Decision: expand, revise or stop against criteria agreed in advance.

slides.transcript: Suppose an operations team wants to reduce service effort while accommodating a new workload. A useful pilot might test one supported configuration under agreed conditions. The team records service steps, workload performance, power and thermal behavior, and support issues. Before starting, it decides who owns each interface and what results would justify expansion. If the evidence misses the criteria, revise the design or stop. That result can still be valuable if it prevents a larger unsuitable deployment.

slides.title: Adopt, participate and contribute at your own scale

bullets.text: Read and compare published work.
Join a relevant discussion with a focused question.
Offer review, test results or operational feedback.

slides.transcript: Your next step might be reading a contribution, attending an open project meeting, talking with a solution provider, or reviewing a draft. You do not need to begin by publishing a complete hardware design. Bring a clear problem and respect the project’s participation and intellectual-property rules. When a question crosses domains, invite the relevant people early. That habit turns individual experience into useful community learning.

term_glossary.tooltip: Design information made available for others to study, use or modify under stated terms. Openness does not itself establish product suitability.
The ability of selected systems or components to work together as required. Shared interfaces support it; an actual configuration still needs validation.
Shared work submitted and published through the applicable OCP process, such as a specification, design or guideline.
An electrical conductor used to distribute power to multiple connections. Its rating and interfaces depend on the design.
Coolant distribution unit: equipment that manages a cooling-loop interface, often including heat exchange and flow control, depending on its design.
A fluid with electrical-insulating properties under its specified conditions. Equipment and materials must be compatible with the chosen fluid.
Keeping products, components and materials useful for longer through approaches such as repair, reuse and recovery.
Product recognition tied to the relevant approved OCP contribution and program requirements; not blanket deployment compatibility or efficiency.
OCP’s facility program using self-certification against its requirements. It does not establish that every workload or configuration is suitable.
